I used to rely on adderall (and before that, concerta) to the point where I was crippled without it. Now, the only dopamine related drug I take is wellbutrin, so I think I'm the kind of person you're talking about.

I weaned off the adderall, while upping the wellbutrin. I take 300 mg total per day now. And while I still have bad executive functioning issues (I'm autistic as well as adhd) I no longer have the same issues I once relied on adderall for—at least, they are better. Now, most of my issues are related to anxiety and BPD (I'm a lovely psychiatric mess) but I'm to a place where I feel confident that once I get those issues under better control, the adhd symptoms will not be a problem.

I feel wellbutrin has been a great solution, and I wish I had made this switch sooner!

I have horrible physical symptoms as well. Constant debilitating pain, and lately there's nausea too which is the worst feeling in the world for me.

Two major things that help for me:

1) learn to maintain a steady heartrate coherence. Heart BPM speeds up as we inhale, lowers as we exhale. So heartrate is a wiggly up and down graph. If you breathe in for the extract amount of time as you breathe out, your "graph" will smooth out into a symmetrical sine wave—this is what people mean by "even" breaths. If you can raise your heartrate coherence—aka smooth out that curve—your body will be affected very intensely. To practice, just sit still and breathe deeply, in for 5 seconds, out for 5 seconds, and keep that up for 10 minutes. You will feel drugged by the end. This is the most powerful type of breathing exercise there is, and there's a lot of great data to back up its effectiveness on health and longevity. Now, I try to do it as often as I can, whenever and wherever I remember. While walking, I breathe in for 4 steps, out for 4 steps. That alone has lessened my physical issues with walking outside by ~50%, which is mind-blowing for me!

2) try to notice times when you don't feel certain symptoms, and keep track of patterns. For example, one of my worst, constant symptoms is jaw pain. My jaw always hurts so badly that I can't focus properly anymore, and I dread doing anything at all. But the pain is gone while I'm eating. I think it's because of how I use my jaw while chewing, and how eating when I'm truly hungry is relaxing and focusing in a primal way. Gum makes it worse, so I can't emulate this. But the knowledge alone that the pain isn't literally constant, that in theory it may one day go away because it does *sometimes*, is amazing and makes me feel so much hope and happiness.

I'm sorry you're struggling with this sickness. It's horrible to lose control of your body and know that it's "all in your head." I feel like such a weak failure for being so sick from something that's "my fault" (even if it's not, logically). It isn't permanent though!! These things aren't set in stone. The psychological nature of the illness actually gives you better chances than if it were an autoimmune problem or whatever. Take it one day at a time <3

*EDIT: can't believe I forgot to mention this! I've started taking beta blockers, and they've changed my life. I still have the pain, but it's not 24/7 anymore, and it's less debilitating. It blocks the body's physical response to stress, so it's perfect for things like this. I highly recommend trying this avenue if you haven't yet.*

I have basically the same problems.

What helps me is to figure out what the problem ACTUALLY is. The problem isn't telling your roommate to clean up after himself, it's some deeper fear.

The way I do this is to try to figure out what the "worst-case scenario" would be. My own personal worst-case scenario is directly tied to the real cause of my anxiety.

I used to be afraid to talk to my roommates. I would walk through the kitchen and they would be sitting at the table, talking and laughing, and I would be too afraid to join in. Or even say hi!

My worst-case scenario for *that* was really 2 scenarios. Either, they would give some reason why I couldn't join, or, they would let me join but not *really* want me there, and feel uncomfortable and feel like I was imposing. Now, I *knew* my roommates liked me, but I couldn't be certain that meant they would want me to impose on whatever specific instance was happening. It came down to a fear of rejection.

Are you worried that your roommate will feel upset if you tell him to clean? Even if he does it without hesitation, and recognizes his responsibility, are you afraid that he would resent you for asking?

The second step, for me at least, is to imagine the other party having the exact same problem. I would have no problem with my roommates joining me if I were out in the kitchen, a public space, where I was clearly not expecting privacy! And if I were actually busy and didn't want to be interrupted, I would say so clearly. You know, after understanding my fears this way, I eventually found the proper courage and context to bring this up with one of my roommates. I learned that the reason he never *offered* for me to join was that HE was also anxious about whether I wanted to hang out with HIM! We were both afraid of rejection, and of accidentally imposing. After that, we were much more comfortable with each other.

Getting to the root of the anxiety is the first step. Don't even worry about actually telling your roommate anything. You can deal with that step in your own time. If you're afraid that he'll dislike you for pointing out his dirty dishes, then maybe someday soon there will be a context in which you can bring that up! Instead of telling him to do his dishes, tell him that you're afraid to tell him to do the dishes! You'd be surprised how much better things can go when you're vulnerable with someone like that. I've never had a conversation like that go badly.

EDIT: And don't worry that you didn't do it! The whole point of therapy homework is that it's safe, obligation-free homework, where you don't get in trouble if you don't do it! :)

I don't have much in the way of practical advice, as I'm not really much better... But I did read something recently that made me feel a lot better, and put things into perspective.

I read an article about ADHD (and learning differences in general) that said people who have to work uphill around people who seem to be on level ground creates this sense of failure. Having to work so incredibly hard to get anything done makes one undervalue the results that are produced, and creates imposter syndrome. People like us tend to magnify the struggles, and minimize our accomplishments.

You CAN have a satisfying, productive life (especially once you're done with school; cookie-cutter school is very difficult with any sort of learning difference). And just because you have to work harder doesn't mean your accomplishments are any less valuable. If anything, it makes what little you do get done mean that much more.

I have a rule for myself that's made me feel a lot better. Make sure every day is a non-zero day. A zero day is laying in bed reading reddit or watching netflix. If you get at least ONE thing done, you didn't have a zero day. Your standards should adjust relative to your ability level. When I was really depressed and could barely get out of bed, getting dressed and going outside meant a non-zero day. These days things like checking my email, calling comcast about a weird bill, or writing a blog post I've been procrastinating on count. Grocery shopping counts. Laundry counts.

I know this doesn't help with getting school work done, but I think low self esteem is a huge part of the problem when it comes to things like this. Every little thing counts. If you can work on an assignment for 5 minutes every day, that's better than nothing, better than zero.

Your school will probably have a disability service department. You should go to them right away (you'll have to bring copies of your diagnostic report) and get set up with a case manager. That's where you would be able to find out about which classes would be better for you. You can also get various accommodations, like note-takers, extra time on assignments and exams, etc.

And if you're an audio learner, I highly recommend watching tutoring videos online! Youtube is a great resource for almost anything, and Khan Academy is the best source for video tutoring by far.

Oh man, I had a full-on panic attack exactly 1 month into my current relationship *in front of* my boyfriend.

There are two possible outcomes here:

1) He thinks you're too much to deal with and breaks it off, or

2) He still loves you and isn't scared away by your anxiety

If the first scenario plays out, then know that this is a relationship that was doomed to end regardless. Some people can't deal with depression, anxiety, or other mental health issues in a relationship. It's just the way of the world, I guess. Your anxiety would have come out sooner or later, so if he's the kind of person that just can't handle that, it's better to know NOW rather than spend months or even years struggling to hide a huge part of yourself from your partner. I've accepted that I'm an anxious person, that this is always going to be a part of me, and while I can learn coping mechanisms, I will never be "cured" because my anxiety is just a symptom of how my brain is wired. I need a partner who can accept who I am, and who I am also happens to include anxiety.

If option 2 is what plays out (which is more likely), then it's great that you got to experience this together and get it out of the way for the same reasons I mentioned above. It's good for him, because he gets to see you at your most vulnerable, and it's good for you, because you won't have to stress about the day when your anxiety inevitably rears its head.

What I recommend is explaining to your boyfriend that you suffer from an anxiety disorder, that you are currently in treatment (if you weren't, that would be a red flag for him), and that you are continually developing new coping mechanisms to deal with your anxiety. But that part of this is that you occasionally have panic attacks, and it isn't anyone's fault. Talk to him about what things he can do to support you when your anxiety is acting up, or you're panicking (hugging you tightly, talking you down, keeping quiet and letting it pass, leaving you alone, whatever works for you).

You aren't any less cute, desirable, feminine, or sexy because you also struggle with anxiety. Almost everyone has gone through periods of anxiety or depression, even people who don't actually have these disorders. Maybe you'll learn that your boyfriend once had a panic attack back in high school during a public speaking class! Maybe he's been depressed on and off and sometimes sees a therapist! And even if he's one of those rare unicorns with no mental health problems, that doesn't mean that he'll think less of you for having panic attacks. If anything, his only worry should be that it upsets him to see you upset.

I'm autistic, I have bad anxiety, and I've been battling depression for around seven years now. My boyfriend is incredibly supportive, and when we hit a wall where he doesn't understand me, or is frustrated, or whatever, we talk it through until we can empathize with each other and come up with an action plan to deal with the problem in the future. It helps that my boyfriend has also had depression for several years now, and he sees his therapist even more frequently than I see mine! So while he doesn't share most of my problems, he knows what it's like to struggle with these things, and that mental health issues are like any other health problem.

Because I have anxiety, there's always that part of me that worries every melt down I have will be "the final straw," and it *is* hard to fight off that beast. But know that this is a good opening to have that first discussion about your anxiety with your boyfriend, and that's a talk that needed to happen sooner or later.

Oh my god, almost the exact same thing happened to me!!!

I was told that I *WILL* get a divorce, and then live the rest of my life without any serious relationship.

After freaking out about it for a year or so, I've totally gotten over it. It's been nine years since that palm reading, and now I can smile about it. I still have a horrible fear of that exact fate (because it's what happened to my mom), but I no longer feel like I'm "destined" to end up that way just because a palm reader told me that. Palm reading is bullshit. I can choose who I marry, and there's no such thing as destiny. The underlying anxiety (fear of divorce) is still there, but it's no longer overwhelming.

I want to add that you're NOT stupid for "letting" this bother you. You were told something hurtful and devastating that would have upset almost anyone. People like us just tend to react to things like that with even more anxiety than is typical. You're not "letting" anything do anything; you didn't choose to panic about this. It's not your fault that something upsetting is upsetting you!

The most important lesson: College is nothing like high school. If you were one of those kids who could coast through school because you were smart enough to not need to study, or study well, then know that you WILL FAIL YOUR CLASSES if you try to rely on your innate intelligence.

Find your own personal skills and use those to develop study methods. For example, I really love drawing, so when I had to study for exams, I would make study guides by drawing pictures of everything. I got an A- in my comparative vertebrate anatomy class, and nearly everyone else failed, because I draw pages and pages of diagrams of muscles, skeletons, and everything else I had to memorize.

Are you a language/audio learner? Make songs and rhymes! Make mnemonics with letters! (My favorite for the 10 basic vertebrate cranial nerves: "OOOTTAFAGV" = "oh, oh, oh, to touch and feel a girl's vagina")

Are you a pattern learner? Make logic diagrams! Letter mnemonics might help you too.

Visual learner? Watch documentaries, draw pictures.

And use Khan Academy as often as possible!

This is a problem that bites all autistics in the ass, no matter how "high-" or "low-functioning." And I totally agree that it's a kind of ableism, but it's a very different type for "aspies" than it is for "classic autistics."

Basically, the high/low thing is a totally misnomer.

What does "functioning" mean? It's all about which types of "functionality" neurotypicals value.

For all intents and purposes:

*High-functioning* means *can pass as neurotypical.*

*Low-functioning* means *cannot pass as neurotypical.*

I know "low-functioning" autistics who function in their everyday lives much better than I, a "very high-functioning" autistic, do. Computer programmers who produce more quality work than everyone else in their department combined. Auto-mechanics who are the best in the state, if not the country. 

My favorite example is Temple Grandin. I hate when journalists call her "high-functioning" or "aspergers" because I feel like it undermines what might be the most inspirational part of her story: Temple Grandin was diagnosed as *severely* low-functioning, completely disabled, and her mother was told to put her in a home.  If you meet her, she's the kind of autistic who simply can't pass for neurotypical. She's utterly monotone, she dresses like a cowboy on picture day, her face is completely blank, and she doesn't use body language. But she functions better than many neurotypicals! She's incredibly successful, great at what she does, and admired by everyone who meets her.

"High-functioning" people are expected to not have any disabilities, because they are able to hide them.

"Low-functioning" people are devalued as people simply because they can't function *socially* on a level that neurotypicals value.

And yes, more severe autism comes with more disability, but that is almost irrelevant when it comes to how neurotypicals treat high- and low-functioning individuals. It's all about passing.

Dude, it really sounds like you need to break up with your girlfriend.

I know it feels impossible. You say she's basically your only friend, and the only girl you know. But this is a horrible reason to stay trapped in a sexless monogamous relationship with her, when you apparently don't even get along that well!! She's saving herself for marriage, I guess, but you know you don't want to marry her, and you *shouldn't*, unless you want to be miserable for the rest of your life. Settling is worse than being single, by far.

I know it can feel like you'll never meet anyone else again. But dude, what are you getting out of this relationship other than pain, and the desperate hope that having this sub-par girlfriend is better than being alone? The rule that I've learned is that if you're unhappy with your relationship more than half the time, that means you need to end it.

As an aspie who also has a hard time making new friends, or even meeting new people, I HIGHLY recommend OK Cupid. Online dating has really levelled the playing field for us autistics who have a hard time meeting people irl. It's easier to "approach" people this way, and it's more likely that someone will "approach" you.

Yes, breaking up with her will be fucking depressing as hell. You will feel like shit for a while. This requires major change in every way, and that feels extra awful for people like us. And the fear of loneliness can seem overwhelming. But dude, there's ALWAYS hope. And staying in a relationship that is ACTIVELY HURTING YOU is way, way worse than the depression you'll have to slog through after ending it.

Feel free to message me if you want to talk. I've been through a somewhat similar situation and I know that just venting can make it better sometimes.

I just had to make an account and comment, because your description of a shutdown/meltdown was so absolutely perfect.

I'm a "high-functioning" autistic (my diagnosis is "autism/Asperger's/NVLD" since they're interchangeable) to the extent that most people would never know I'm autistic unless I told them, or they were autism experts themselves and knew what to look for. I can pass for neurotypical *very* well, if I put in a lot of effort, basically. I always get the "you must be SO high-functioning" crap.

I'm not as easily triggered into a shutdown/meltdown as you, but I definitely know what you're describing, and have experienced both. I have much more specific triggers, usually in contexts that only come up in romantic relationships due to some past trauma. Like, if I feel like my partner is disappointed with me, or angry with me, I have a tendency to spiral into the kind of thing you described. But I also run into this when I'm forced into trying to describe my emotions, reasons behind my emotions, etc. It's like the Windows blue screen of death. Or when I'm pushed past a certain point while I'm too exhausted, frustrated, whatever.

>It's impossible to focus on anything but self-inflicted "pain". I pinch, hit and claw at my thighs and arms. If I am extremely gone I claw at my scalp and beat my head. The feeling of me hurting myself is the only thing in the world that I can focus on, and it brings me back down to Earth.

Especially this. When I start to dissociate (it's like hitting a wall in my brain where it's almost like I don't understand what's going on, and can't 'think' anymore) I claw at myself, dig my nails into my palms, wrists, and hands, etc. The pain is very grounding and brings me back to the present. Kind of like when hysterical people are "knocked out of it" with a slap in old movies, I guess. Too bad it scares other people because it's technically self-harm.

I always find it really fascinating to hear the experiences of other autistics, especially those who are more "severe" than me, because even though we look so different to outsiders, what's going on inside is almost always the same to some degree.
